utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please, for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, Michael McVicker with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have to recall that the accused himself has waived his right to be present for the first moments of the hearing of the witness before us. First of all, good afternoon to you, Witness. And may we please hear your solemn declaration. Please stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And the OTP may start the examination-in-chief, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, would you please tell the Court what your name is.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: My name is Nusret Sivac. I was born on the 19th of August, 1947 in Prijedor, where I lived all my life until 1992. On several occasions, such my military service or my schooling, I was absent from Prijedor, but only for brief periods of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Sivac, as I've explained to you, we have been requested to perform a little identification exercise at the moment. Five individuals are going to enter the Court. I would ask you to please -- six, excuse me, six individuals. I'd ask you to please note the position of those individuals with the one-- they will be standing on your left. And as you turn towards your left, the person farthest to your right will be the first, that should be the first person to enter. And the person last to enter who will be farthest to your left, will be number 6. They're going to be in court and walking and if you have any request to have them repeat any motion or gesture, you may make that request. The purpose is to see if you recognise any of those six individuals. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We will not ask you for your opinion until after they have left the courtroom. So you will not have to speak until after they have left. So at the present time, the individuals will enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish to have this in open session or private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we discussed this matter, and the parties agreed to do this in closed session. So therefore, please, closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I already now take the opportunity to announce that it will be necessary, immediately after the break, to discuss some urgent matters as regards the case and the scheduling order. And therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, did Your Honour receive -- I don't know if you want to wait for Mr. Stakic to be here. Perhaps I should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's necessary to do it in the presence of all the participants and Dr. Stakic immediately after the break, only to inform you that we can't continue immediately with our witness after the break. [The accused entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic, you have been informed by your own Defence counsel on the outcome of this identification parade?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please, be seated. And the OTP may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, before the accused was in court, you indicated that you were born in 1947 in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Had your family lived in Prijedor for long before that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, for about 300 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted, but we missed your last comment.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, 300 years, about 300 years, that's how long my family had lived in Prijedor for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your ethnicity? What do you identify yourself as?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak and a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married. I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How old were your children in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: My son was 6, and my daughter was 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is your wife also a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what was your profession prior to the 1990s, let's say?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Prior to 1990, I worked for a year in the Ljubija iron ore mine, and then I started working for the security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say the security services, would it be correct to say that in Bosnia and in the former Yugoslavia, the State Security Service was divided into two general parts, one being the regular police, and one being state security?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, mainly, you could break it down like that. The security service was usually divided into a number of sectors. And that depended and changed from time to time. It all depended on how the security service was organised at the republic level, what sort of decisions were made in Sarajevo in the SUP, the republican secretariat for the interior. The organisation of local security services were articulated there. In Prijedor, for a while, you only had the municipal SUP with competencies only in Prijedor municipality, and then for a while you had the regional for the security service. When I say that, it was the security service for the areas around Prijedor also, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Sanski Most, and so on. With time, the hierarchy and the structure in Prijedor changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For what years did you work for the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Look, the service I worked for was the communications and crypto-security centre or the communications centre. That was the abbreviation we used. And then through different transformations, first, it belonged to the State Security Service, and then by a new organisational scheme, it was part of the public security service. So, the centre where I worked was transferred from one type of organisation to a totally new scheme, in order to serve the general needs of the security services in Bosnia and Herzegovina and within the larger framework of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So forgive me for misusing the term, but for what years did you work in the security services, meaning whatever way it was organised? For what years did you work for that organisation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Since 1973, until the end of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you worked in a specialty of communications and encryption. Does that mean that you were in charge of sending messages between the local station and higher authorities? Was that part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well yes, but my centre, the communications centre within the security service served all the different security services in Prijedor Municipality, and even in a wider area. I'm referring to the surrounding municipalities, local communes. And we did missions of importance for the state and for the republic, for the different segments, within the municipality in the committee we worked for the post, for the Territorial Defence, for the secretariat for national defence, for all the different bodies of authority in Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to take advantage of your experience with the security service to ask you some questions about how that operated in Prijedor. I believe after the 1990 elections, the chief of police for Prijedor was Mr. Talundzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, the chief was Talundzic, yes, yes. Hasan Talundzic. Hasan Talundzic was appointed chief of the security services upon the proposal of the Party of Democratic Action, and that was a unique case. Up to that point, and I must emphasise this, the head of the Security Services Centre was never a Muslim, and that was the first time a Muslim was appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct that after the takeover by the SDS, Mr. Drljaca replaced Mr. Talundzic? You can just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My question, sir, is if you could help us by discussing your knowledge of the relationship between the head of the Prijedor SUP in the normal operations throughout your career and the president of the municipality of Prijedor? Would there be any interaction between those two positions?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, no one could be the chief of the security services in Prijedor Municipality without his appointment having been approved by the president of Prijedor Municipality and other segments of authority within Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In your experience, was it common for the chief of the SUP to keep the president of the municipality informed about major events occurring in the work of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in my time and later, as far as I could tell, all security and information situations in Prijedor Municipality, how many crimes had happened, traffic infractions, and all other criminal actions in the municipality, both the president of the municipality and the president of the Municipal Assembly were regularly informed. And the assembly discussed these issues in its regular sessions. For a while, the Municipal Assembly even published a gazette, an Official Gazette, on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. security situation in Prijedor Municipality over 10 or 15 days or a month and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, why did you leave your position with the security services in 1989?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Parallel to my work for the security service, I started work for TV Sarajevo. I sent reports from Prijedor and the surroundings of Prijedor. Due to the interhuman relationships and due to the fact that Milos Jankovic was appointed the head of my section, whose task was to ethnically cleanse my section, the section of the services in which I worked. May I please draw Your Honours' attention to the following fact: My service was one of the most delicate services within the security services, and until Milos Jankovic was appointed, there was rigorous control over how many people were employed and about their national background. But when Milos Jankovic was appointed, a friend of mine, a colleague of mine, Esad Vojnikovic was fired from the services for a trivial reason. And after Esad Vojnikovic had been fired, he was one of the man encrypters, one of the ablest people for that sort of job. Milos Jankovic started a number of verbal, at first, and then physical, duels with me. I couldn't cope with this, why stand this, so I resigned from my position within the security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You indicated that, parallel to your work for the service, you worked as a journalist for TV Sarajevo. Is it correct that as part of your duties -- let me start again. Can you tell us in your work as a journalist for TV Sarajevo, what were the duties that you had? What kind of events would you cover?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, mostly, I worked as a cameraman. I made independent coverages, and we covered all the segments of life in Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, that part of Bosanska Krajina, all segments of life, all aspects of life, culture, sports, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you cover events in the political life of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's one thing I forgot to say. And very often, I did cover events from politics in Prijedor Municipality and the surrounding municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Through your work, did you become familiar with some of the political figures in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was unavoidable. We were in close contact with the politicians who were in power. We often conducted interviews with them. We made special features, special coverages regarding the political situation in Prijedor. And what should be done in order to improve this situation and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, have you ever been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I have. We had to be members of the Communist League. Nobody who was involved in this sensitive type of work could do this work, could have this kind of job without being a member of the Communist League.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understand. After the multiparty system came into place in 1990, did you join any of the political parties, either the descendants of the communist party or any of the leftist or nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of any such party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of any paramilitary organisation or any secret organisation tied to any national parties or national group?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you cover a political event that was, I believe, the first rally of the SDS in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The first rally of the Serb democratic party for the Prijedor Municipality was held on the Ilinden holiday on the 2nd of August, 1991, the village of Maricka in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the year the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What year did that event take place in, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It took place in the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a village named Maricka. Is that outside of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is very close to Omarska, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the history of Prijedor as you know it, did that particular part of Prijedor have any political history different from other parts of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In a way, yes. How shall I put this? The Prijedor Municipality was unofficially divided during the Second World War. One part of the municipality, above the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road and the railway line, that is, the mid-part of the area, which gravitates to the Kozara Mountain was pre-dominantly pro-partisan, whereas the southern part, the villages around the town of Omarska, such as Maricka, Jelicka, Krivaje, were rather pro-Chetnik in their orientation. And in the Second World War and at the end of the Second World War, there were a large number of people who sided with the Chetniks from that area. In school in Prijedor for about 50 years, they taught us that no Chetnik had ever managed to enter the Kozara Mount, but unfortunately, they were very active in the southern parts of the municipality around the villages of Maricka, Jelicka and other villages in the area of Omarska. And the Chetnik warlords were quite famous, Rade Rajic [phoen], Vaso Mijatovic, Drenovac, who was very known at the time and other Chetnik warlords were very active in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just occurred to me that the proofing note I prepared this morning which I gave to the Defence before court, I had not yet distributed to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think actually we got it. It's telephone notes or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, no, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In addition. Okay. Thank you. Thank you for this courtesy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that first SDS rally - you said it took place in 1990 - do you recall some of the more recognisable personalities that were present, that spoke at that rally?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: One of the key figures at the time was Jovan Raskovic, leader of the Serbs from Knin. Apart from him, the entire leadership of the Serb Democratic Party was present there, those who were later to hold their rally in Sarajevo. In particular, Karadzic, Plavsic, and others. And other supporters from the SDS from the area of Prijedor and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sivac, we started today when you pointed out Dr. Stakic. In 1990, was Dr. Stakic someone that you knew?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately, I didn't know Dr. Stakic in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: After the first democratic elections, after the key political offices were distributed in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to go now to the events of 1992. On the 30th of April of 1992, first, can you tell the Court in what area of Prijedor did you live?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I lived in Marsala Tito Street in the centre of Prijedor town, on the main street in Prijedor, house number 25. The building in question was located near the old mosque that once stood in the centre of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be helpful if S3 be placed on the ELMO, that is, the map of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so. It could also be of assistance if the other map, I think it's S14, be placed on the ELMO that we can identify Maricka on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The image is not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We're testing your eyesight in many ways today, Mr. Sivac.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But this is not a complete town map. As far as I can see, this is the Bosanski Novi/Prijedor railway line. I can see the northern parts of the town, Puharska and Urije. To the right, I can see Keraterm, the football stadium, and the new residential area around the football stadium. And as for the old part of the town, I don't know. Did you want me to point out to the street where I lived?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The main street in Prijedor, must be here, in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, indicating --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It's here in parallel with this street which ends up at the Prijedor Hotel. This is not a very well marked map. It's difficult to make out --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: -- the details, but it's in this part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The Witness indicated, he said parallel to the street where the Hotel Prijedor is. You can see the Hotel Prijedor just before the river, and I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct that that street's name was Uliza Yugoslav [phoen] or Yugoskan [phoen]? It's very difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The street that was perpendicular to the Prijedor hotel, I think was called Mira Cikota Street. However, after the takeover the SDS and the Prijedor Municipality leadership changed a number of street names. So I don't know whether this map was from that period of time, that is, after the takeover or before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How far away was the mosque from your house?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Up to 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how far away was Stari Grad, the beginning of Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: From my place? Maybe 800 to 1.000 metres away from my place. That's where the Stari Grad began. Maybe even closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, if we could have the other map marked brought out. I believe -- okay. Yes, the lower right is the area around Omarska. Perhaps the map could be centered more around Omarska.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Are we now looking for the village of Maricka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This is Maricka, this area here. It actually consists of a number of hamlets, but they are commonly referred to as Maricka. The whole area is called Maricka, this area here, below the Omarska mine. So the east, there is a fish pond, a large fish pond in Sanicani, and south east, we find the Tomasica mine, Busnovi, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to the record is clear, the transcript, you've indicated an area. Perhaps I can give us the names of some of the towns in that area. Are you saying, for example, from Muzicka to the west, Miodragovici in the northwest to approximately around Stakici in this area, east?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Vuckovic, Mikanovici, Radici, this whole area here including Grubani, Radici, these are the names of a number of families that are named after these villages. Actually, it's probably the villages that got named after the families who lived there. Kabici, for instance, is the place where most of the people are called Kabici. Markovici, Grabezi, Mikanovici, Majstorovici, Grubani, Zrnici; these are all family names of the local families, people who lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The interpreters haven't complained, but if I could ask you to speak a little bit slower for their benefit, so we don't lose anything.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the 30th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm done with the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the events of the 30th of April, 1992, Mr. Sivac, can you tell us when you became aware of a change in Prijedor that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It happened in the early morning hours in the street where I lived. We could hear, all of a sudden, voices of the soldiers and we could tell that there was a commotion down there. Military APCs passed along the street, and at first, we didn't realise what was going on in Prijedor. A Serb neighbour of mine, a lady neighbour of mine, came to my apartment, and she told us to turn on the radio and find the local Prijedor station and listen to the news that were being broadcast by the station at the time. Which is what we did immediately. We switched on the radio, and we listened to the Prijedor station which was playing Chetnik songs. But there was also an announcement that was read over the radio, an announcement which spoke about the fact that the Serb Democratic Party had taken over all power in Prijedor, that it was no longer possible to wait, that the Serb -- that the Party for Democratic Action, which had been in power in the Prijedor Municipality, was destroying Prijedor, and that it was impossible for the members of the Serb Democratic Party who shared power with them, to find any agreement whatsoever with the SDA, that there was a total chaos in the municipality, and that that was the reason why the people from the SDS, assisted by the military and the police, had carried out a military coup, that they had taken control of all vital positions, vital points in and out of the town Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of Prijedor, and that from that time on, the Serb Democratic Party would be in power in Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. It's not -- thank you for slowing down, but it's not necessary to do to pause quite as much as you did. They are very quick, the interpreters. You can speak in a normal voice, but just take care not to speak too quickly. Do you recall any political figure speaking on the radio that day or in the days soon after that regarding the takeover?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, sometime during that day, the listeners of the Prijedor radio station had an opportunity of hearing the new president of the Prijedor Municipality, Mr. Milomir Stakic, who, in his speech, repeated everything that had already been said in this announcement I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to skip to the 12th of May. On the 12th of May, were you still living in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 12th of May, I was still in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On that day, did something happen to you? And if so, can you please explain to us what happened.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Two men from the security service came to my apartment, two individuals whom I knew very well. One was called Pravoslav Sekulic and the other Neso Babic. They said that they had an order to take me to the Security Services Centre. When I came to the security service, to their offices, I was taken to their chief whose name was Ranko Mijic. Ranko Mijic used to be the chief of the crime department in the Prijedor SUP. He was very rude. He said that he had been issued with an order by the new Serb authorities and the Crisis Staff to seize all of my equipment, the equipment that I needed for my work as a reporter for the Sarajevo TV. I knew him very well. And I asked him whether it could wait a little, that I needed some time to collect all this equipment that he had asked for. But he was very adamant. He said that all the equipment should be returned immediately. And he appointed, apart from the two individuals that had taken me there, two more men who took me to the premises of the Sarajevo TV station, and we found there the equipment that I used for the purposes of my work as a reporter. After that, I was taken back to the security service where I stayed for a while. I didn't know what would happen with me. And one of the guards told me that I would probably be taken to the prison in Stara Gradiska. However, after a number of brief telephone consultations, with I don't know whom, Ranko Mijic came out, and he said that those who had taken me into custody should take me back home. He said that I should not leave Prijedor, that they would have some additional questions to ask of me, but later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what equipment or property that -- did you have that was confiscated on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The usual equipment, which all local news agencies had in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It consisted of a large vehicle adequately equipped with cameras and additional property which is necessary for TV coverages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the vehicle was also confiscated in addition to the video and electronic equipment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was. Everything, even some of my private tapes. I was a film amateur. I had covered the life of Prijedor town for quite some time on an amateur videocamera. But everything was confiscated, and I'm very sorry because I had a lot of such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to the events of the 30th of May of 1992. Do you recall that day, and did you become aware sometime during that day of some unusual events taking place?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I will never forget that day. I don't think that any resident of the Prijedor will ever forget that day. I noticed in the evening hours of that day that the situation had calmed down in the town. Before that, there had been a lot of noise, a lot of commotion. But all of a sudden, everything was very quiet, and I noticed from the surrounding high-rise buildings which were located in the vicinity of my house, I noticed that there were no longer any Serb soldiers and snipers on those skyscrapers, because from the beginning of the takeover, they were there, closely following the situation in the town and the movement of the population there. They were on the roofs of those skyscrapers. So this quiet was rather unusual, and I thought that perhaps the new authorities were trying to bring the life back to normal, and that that was the reason why they removed those soldiers who had been positioned on the roofs of those skyscrapers. And I thought that they would also remove the machine-gun nests that had been put in place in front of a number of major buildings in the town. But it turned out that the situation was completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Around 4.00 in the morning, on the 30th of May, at dawn, a group of people headed by Slavko Ecimovic who, after the takeover of the SDS, were exposed to a number of threats. Slavko Ecimovic's house had been attacked a number of times with hand grenades. He was persecuted by Serb police officers -- actually, he had been persecuted by Serb police officers. And at one point in time, he went to the Kurevo woods with a group of people from Prijedor, mainly the people who had failed to respond to the mobilisation which was carried out en masse by what was already a Serb army. Some of those people were sacked and dismissed from work. So after the takeover, they knew that they could no longer live normally in Prijedor. And that they would be severely punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sivac, but for reasons of time mainly, I want to go just to the attack if you can describe what you saw at that time.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, at 4.00, at 4.00, in Prijedor, shooting began, terrible shooting. We didn't know what was going on. We didn't know that Slavko Ecimovic and his group tried to, as they said, liberate Prijedor. We turned on the radio again to listen to Prijedor radio station, and we heard announcements and songs that we had never heard up to that point. Radical Chetnik songs calling for the killing of Turks and other non-Serb people, announcements read by speakers of Radio Prijedor whom I had known very well, Senija Dzafic, a Muslim lady, Jadranka Vejo, unfortunately also a Muslim lady. Those announcements informed the Serb people about Muslim extremists led by Slavko Ecimovic having attacked the town of Prijedor. The announcements said that all those Serbs who had been assigned weapons should stand up and defend the town. The group led by Slavko Ecimovic, they said, should be destroyed. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said you heard the shooting beginning at 4.00. Did the -- was the shooting that you heard, was it small arms or heavier weapons and did it change during the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, at the beginning it was just light infantry weapons. Slavko's people, people from Slavko's group had such weapons. Later on, the unequal confrontation between Slavko's group and the Prijedor SUP members and the Serb army led by Zoran Karlica and Radmilo Zeljaja, Slavko Ecimovic's people did not stand a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did you see from where you were? I presume, was it correct, you were in your apartment throughout this day until taken outside?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the flat for the whole time, and I saw roughly how the fighting on the main street developed, how Slavko's people retreated towards the Sana River in a bid to leave Prijedor because they realised that they were powerless to achieve anything in the town. They were already being followed by the frantic, in a manner of speaking, defenders of Prijedor with their APCs, with their tanks. And with a large number of heavy artillery weapons which they even mounted outside my building. That's how they defended the old town in Prijedor and the other parts of Prijedor where mostly Muslims lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened, then? Did the --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, after -- I mean, in the early hours of the morning, the ethnic cleansing, let me say, of the town of Prijedor began. With all the artillery weapons they had and a very large number of soldiers, the Serbs encircled section by section of the town. I saw when they brought people in long columns outside my building from the Raskovac and Skela area. They were all moving in a column two by two. They had white straps on their arms, and each column was led by a man carrying a white flag. They were escorted by brutal guards. There were many elderly people and children, people who couldn't move. They just pushed them along in wheelchairs. They were brought to certain places where buses arrived to pick these people up and take them away, some to Trnopolje, some to Omarska camp, and some to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see any areas that the tanks or artillery were firing upon, or did you see any portions of the city burning from your apartment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, almost for the whole day until late in the afternoon, from those positions outside my house, the bank of the Bereg, for a long time a tank and several grenade launchers were firing upon the old town. The old town was ablaze since the early morning hours. Allow me please to mention that the old town is actually the old core that the town developed from. There were over 200 houses there built from the ancient Bosnian style. Muslims were the predominant population in the old town. There was only a single Serb family living in the old town. Of course, the first to be struck in the old town and in Zagrad, the Bereg part of the town, were the mosques. Both mosques had been hit and destroyed and burned during the first -- the initial onslaught.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that they were hit during the initial onslaught. Did you see any mosque or church damaged after the initial fighting?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In the evening hours roughly, I saw a very good acquaintance of mine, Milenko Milic, who was a member of Milan Andzic's paramilitary unit. With him was his commander, Momcilo Radanovic, Cigo, and Milorad Vokic, a professional police officer, who was a personal bodyguard to Simo Drljaca. At 6.00 in the afternoon on the 30th of May, they entered the yard outside the main mosque in the town of Prijedor and set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did anyone come to your apartment that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: That day, a number of soldiers came on a number of occasions with red berets, with red straps, with red hats. They were wearing all kinds of insignia, so I couldn't quite make out which unit those soldiers belonged to. They were searching flats for weapons, not only my flat but also other flats for valuables. They were looking for alcohol, and that's what they would then take and carry off with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did they come into your apartment and take valuables or alcohol?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they entered my flat, my neighbour's flat, too. Mostly Muslim flats, and they would take whatever they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was your family at home?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The whole time, my wife was with me, my son, who was 6, and my daughter, who was 11. They cried and screamed. They were scared out of their wits really, and it was really difficult to put up with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That day, were there any announcements on the radio that you heard giving instructions to Serb or Croat residents of the Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were several announcements warning -- informing non-Serb population to put out white flags on their houses and flats so that non-Serbs, that's the term I will use, would be made to wear white straps on their arms. And that until further notice, they would not be allowed to move freely around the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you remain in your apartment the entire day, or were you asked to go out on the street?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: At one point, a group of soldiers arrived led by a Serb soldier wearing a red beret. Another had a Chetnik Subara for a hat. He had a beard, and the others wore black bands, headbands, around their heads. Although I knew many people in Prijedor, I had never seen anyone from that group up to that point. And they ordered all Muslims to leave the building and wait outside the entrance. There was only my family left in that house who were Muslims, and the flat below mine belonged to Safet Ramadanovic, a neighbour of mine, and his family. We came out and they made us turn around, our face -- our faces to the wall. And the commander said: "Should anyone move, mow them down." But we were quite lucky because at that time, Milorad Vokic was passing by. He was an old policeman from Prijedor, and he walked up to the commander who was wearing a red beret, and he told him something. And then the commander told us to go back to our flats. Milorad Vokic then spoke to me and Safet, and he said: "I saved your lives now, but should your name appear on any arrest list, I will not be able to help you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you later see your neighbour Safet in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Safet Ramadanovic, an elderly person, he was soon after taken to Omarska. And I witnessed his death in the camp, death which came as a result of the beatings that he had been subjected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time to break. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Trial stands adjourned until 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. First of all, I have to inform you on the development in the case of Mr. Mrdja, which would have an impact on the case before us as regards the schedule. I was informed last week by a memo sent by Ms. Joanna Korner, that the OTP is prepared to proceed with the Prosecution's case in chief in that case, Mrdja case, on 1 October 2002. As I said earlier, the next prerequisite would be to have the assignment of ad litem Judges or permanent Judges to this other case to be heard in a break of this case. I have to inform you that on requesting so, the 25th of July, the President informed me as followed, and please take this document as a new J document. And I would ask you to read this document out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Document J11. [Interpretation] "Dear colleague, following your oral request of the 25th of July, 2002, I would like to inform you that the case Mrdja has been referred to the International Tribunal and could be heard in October this -- could not be heard in October this year because of nonavailability of the judge. "Sincerely signed, Claud Jorda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The background has to be explained a little bit. First, there was policy, in the past there was only one policy. There's a policy to assign ad litem Judges to one case only, as the word "ad litem" and not ad lites, plural, indicates already. I have to accept this decision by the President, and this means that we have to hear this case without any break. And we find the words in parenthesis, it is linked evidently to a presentation, the President of this Tribunal gave on behalf of this Tribunal at the Security Council last week indicating that in future, only cases against the main responsible ones should be heard here in The Hague. This will cause some problems, no doubt. But we have to discuss this in the framework of the case Prosecutor versus Mrdja. In addition to that, I was informed today in this other case that there, the Defence would not be prepared to start the Defence case without a break of additional two months after having heard the Prosecutor's case. Additional problems rose there due to the fact that the Defence counsel himself as he said "used to be the republic Prosecutor of Republika Srpska in the period of 20.3.1998, to 20.3.2002." This means -- the meaning for our case, and this is an additional background for the President's decision to act as he did. It was the fear that this case could be additionally delayed, and therefore, it's indispensable that we stick to the scheduling deadlines in the scheduling order of 4 July 2002, without any additional break or delay. Any observations as regards this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Not for this case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for your information, I separately summoned a Status Conference the last week of September. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, in response to your question with respect to the scheduling that would commence in -- namely the Defence case in chief commencing on the 11th of November, I believe, based on the schedule offered on the 4th of July of this year, in light of the fact that the Defence will be bringing all of its witnesses from a third country or another country, unlike the OTP, who has in-house witnesses who they can call at a shorter notice, we would like at the very least for the Court to consider, and perhaps give us an opportunity, such as in the OTP's case in chief to suspend the proceedings from going forward on either alternate Fridays or every Friday. It would give the Defence, we believe, an opportunity to coordinate better with the witnesses because it will give us a chance to meet with them and discuss the aspects of it and be more efficient. Likewise, it would give us an opportunity to reflect back on the testimony and make the Defence strategy necessary, in order to meet between ourselves as counsel and also to meet with our client Dr. Stakic. We think especially in the Defence case, it is imperative that we consult with Dr. Stakic even more so than we have when the witnesses were called from the Prosecution. Namely, because we did get in advance some of the statements. And in our defence, we necessarily would not have the exhaustive, because of the equality of arms issues, statements, we are still in the process of compiling them. And with the assistance of Dr. Stakic, we would request that in the very least as in the OTP's case we be given alternate Fridays, if not every Friday off, so we can efficiently produce the witness and conduct our Defence in a manner prescribed by the rules. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I think this is a fair approach, and also from the perspective of the Bench, maybe also the OTP, it seems adequate to have at least one day during the week for thinking and not only acting. And therefore, we will take care that there will always be a possibility of acting this way. But please understand that I can't already now tell you when there will be such a Friday off, but it starts already the 15th of November, court maintenance day, first Friday. Then the 5th of December, United Nations holiday. Friday, the 6th of December, there will be a so-called bridge day, no court. And as regards the other days, we will have to decide on a case-by-case basis, but we will let you know in advance. Having said this, we have made reservation for this courtroom during the entire period. Therefore, if the Defence believes it would make sense, we could even - we discussed this this morning - we could even hear the first witness already one week before. It's only an invitation. And in addition, I have to reemphasise that that what can be read in the beginning of this scheduling order is still valid, the invitation to come, if not in toto but then in part to an agreement in this case because listening to the parties, I'm aware that numerous details contested in the past are no longer really contested. And therefore, it seems really appropriate if both parties come together and try to come to a kind of at least part -- agreement in part. But the most crucial point is that if we can't shorten in any event, we have to stick to this scheduling order as it was planned. And the fact, mere fact that we cannot hear five days a week is not a reason to postpone or to prolong the case. Then I have to turn back to another issue. As regards the documents already admitted into evidence, the entire bundle of documents S235, this is the document seize -- the bundle of documents seized by Witness O'Donnell we heard the last day. We had the impression that it is the Defence case here to try to contest the admissibility of this evidence under the doctrine of the fruit of the poisoned tree. Therefore, we have to rethink this issue, and we invite the parties to give their observations to the admissibility in the obvious absence of a search and seizure order in this case, a problem we always have in these cases. In the absence, once again, of rules governing the investigation, and this is for the simple reason that, normally, in the beginning, it was the intention of the drafters of our statute and our rules that one could rely on the Rules of Procedure and Evidence or the code of criminal procedure in the requested country to work on this basis there, which is not the case on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and rules had to be developed. But for these reasons, we reopen the discussion on the admissibility of this evidence. For the Defence, contesting this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we continue to maintain our objection, that the material disclosed should not be admissible for several reasons as outlined previously in our oral presentation to the Court. However, not only does the fruit of the poisonous tree play an enormous part here, we believe that in addition to that, irreversible harm has been caused by the OTP offering such a document and insinuating, without laying a proper foundation, that the originals of those documents were somehow returned to Dr. Stakic. We take great exception to the OTP testifying on this fact and continued to demand from them that they present to us the individuals who claim that they returned the original documents back to Dr. Stakic. My learned friend Mr. Koumjian advised the Court last week that he's asking for a certain search could be conducted of the Detention Unit of Dr. Stakic so as to avoid him being present, so that they can find the documents, again leading in my opinion respectfully to an inappropriate impression or inference that the OTP would like to present. Those documents, Your Honour, have never been established by the OTP to have been returned to Dr. Stakic. Now, upon having the search being fully conducted, and admittedly initially inappropriately for whatever the reasons, conducted subsequently not having found those original documents, I think it casts a significant cloud, not only on the very documents that are sought to be presented, but on the very testimony that the OTP claims their expert may have an opinion. Specifically, the OTP has stated that they needed original signatures in order for there to be any relevance or credibility to their expert handwriting witness. Those documents don't exist for whatever reason. We are in great dispute with them as to where the originals of those documents are. However, as we heard from Mr. Bernard O'Donnell last week, admittedly he is a professional who has, I'm sure, great credentials in connection with criminal investigations, he acknowledged not only that improperly, in our opinion, those documents were seized, they were never inventoried. A highly irregular and unusual procedure for an investigator of his calibre working with this Tribunal. Had the documents been at the very least inventoried, not by providing a detailed description but merely stating the name of the document as reflected on the top, indicating whether or not the document is signed, and then providing Dr. Stakic with a sheet of paper, having him sign to indicate this chain of custody, which is not only important in this proceeding but in any proceeding across the world. We feel that these documents should not be admissible for those reasons as well as the reasons we have cited previously. We think the OTP has failed to lay the proper foundation, has inappropriately caused inferences to be made as a result of these documents. And by their own admission through their witnesses, have not only cast the doubt but have confirmed that the documents were seized illegally, inappropriately, and without the consent of Dr. Stakic. So we would ask that they be inadmissible or not admitted. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate the creative advocacy by my opponent. I would like to address several of those issues, first of all, at the end of the argument that there was no inventory of the documents. In fact, that's not the testimony of Mr. O'Donnell. The documents, every single page, was photocopied, and that's what is in exhibit, I believe the number is 235. The entire -- all those photocopies were entered -- given to the evidence unit, and we have them. What we don't have are the originals, and I use that word to mean the documents that were actually in Dr. Stakic's bag, because I can't say for sure that those were originals or whether he had photocopies of some of those documents. For the Defence to say that there's absolutely no reason for us or no evidence that these were returned to Dr. Stakic, well, the evidence will come, if necessary, from the registry, the evidence will be that the registry was given through the OLAD unit the documents. Part of those documents the Defence knows were returned to Mr. Lukic. We can put on evidence, I don't think the Defence is contesting that, of a signed receipt from Mr. Lukic. I'm not saying that one of the eight pages that are in dispute containing the signatures were in those. But we have a receipt from Mr. Lukic for car keys, car registration, and at least one of the documents - the receipt was not that specific - that are in these 81 pages. I don't think that's contested by the Defence. As far as the fruit of the poisonous tree doctrine is, Your Honour, there is no poisonous tree in this case. In the legal system I am most familiar with and in my, admittedly somewhat rudimentary, knowledge of other systems, all the systems I know, items that are on the person of a person arrested may be seized without a further order. We had an arrest warrant in this case for Dr. Stakic. The reason that legal systems recognise that these items can be seized without further search orders is that, first, to prevent their destruction. And that's, in fact -- this is a good example of it, perhaps, in this case. We are not saying that we are going to prove that Dr. Stakic intentionally destroyed these documents. What we do say is that the documents were returned to the OLAD unit which indicates that they passed these on, and we don't have them any more. Admittedly, many of these are rather innocuous, so we can't say why they were not retained, they were not found in Dr. Stakic's cell. Further, another reason why documents are allowed to be seized is second, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to prevent any claim that the police have stolen documents or planted documents on an accused. It's important, during the arrest, to document those items that were on the accused at the time of his arrest. So when a person is booked, as we say, following his arrest, it's important that all of those items he had on him are taken into evidence or taken into custody, which was the case here. In fact, the items were not seized except to be photocopied, and then they were returned to Dr. Stakic. So this procedure prevented any claim that anything had been stolen from him. So for these reasons, I think in almost any jurisdiction, items that are in the immediate possession of an accused may be retained in evidence. There is no exclusionary rule in this Tribunal other than a rule, which I'm sorry I don't know the number off the top of my head, which indicates that the Court may exclude items where it offends the -- the means in which they were acquired is offensive to the administration of justice. Or words to that effect. I think this is hardly the case here. Your Honours have heard from the tape, how Mr. O'Donnell - from the transcript of the tape - treated Dr. Stakic. He was allowed to take medicine from his bag. This bag contained these documents. These documents were then photocopied, and then returned to the OLAD unit. This is not offensive to the administration of justice. In fact, this shows a very careful procedure that's respectful of the rights of the accused. I think -- my only criticism would be it went too far. The OTP, perhaps, should have retained the originals and should not have returned those to the accused. But it certainly is not offensive that the items were taken and photocopied, and the photocopies retained by the OTP. I also want to make the record clear that we think that the photocopies themselves have great evidentiary value. Clearly, if there were originals with signatures, that would much preferable on the part of the handwriting expert. But the handwriting comparison expert can sometimes make use of photocopies. And further, even outside of that, it's very relevant to the issue of the type of signature, the manner in which Dr. Stakic would sign his name which would be signing "S. Milomir" or "Milomir," rather than Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand you made reference to Rule 95. This is the exclusive rule in our rules on procedure and evidence for the exclusion of certain evidence. And only under these circumstances laid down there, evidence may be excluded. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any observations in return?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, with respect to the three points raised by the OTP, first of all, we should not look at this situation or this Tribunal as a typical setting that counsel may be familiar with, whether in the United States or any jurisdiction. Truly, when an investigator arrests or tries to make an arrest on an individual of a crime, it happens not ten years later. His theory and arguments and logic in connection with destruction of evidence simply baffles me, with respect to claiming that evidence with respect to Dr. Stakic's personal medical forms or dental forms or prescriptions that he is taking would lead to any significant evidence here. If the arrest was made contemporaneous with or near the time of events as alleged in the indictment, perhaps that argument would hold some water. I do not believe that it does. I do, and must admit, that I admire the courage of the OTP to suggest that that there were documents or arguing that planting of documents does occur from time to time with respect to police investigators and individuals who may try to incarcerate suspects under indictment. The simple matter, Your Honour, is that we will not, and probably cannot, prove any such theory in this case with respect to Mr. O'Donnell's evidence and testimony. We do, however, find his testimony on a personal and professional level to be very offensive, unlike the OTP. Offensive, because Mr. O'Donnell clearly stated both on the tape, and on the written transcript that he provided, that he advised Dr. Stakic of his right to remain silent and encouraged him at one point before the illegal search began of his bag that he will no longer ask him any questions until after his legal representative would be appointed to him. As I believe the record reflects, not less than ten minutes after advising Dr. Stakic again of his right and advising Dr. Stakic that he would have legal representation, did Mr. O'Donnell perform this illegal search and this illegal taking of Dr. Stakic's personal bag and belongings. Planting of documentation, as the OTP states, is an important protocol that most criminal investigators follow. However, the protocol that should have been followed was not as it relates to Mr. O'Donnell. Any jurisdiction, no matter how sophisticated, trains their police and investigators to inventory the documents that are seized, to make a list of the documents that were taken, to advise the person from whom you're taking those documents what it is that you're taking, and to seek from them a signature, so that there can be no disagreement as to what those documents or items or personal effects were that the police or investigator confiscated. In this case, I believe the evidence is clear that we did not, and Mr. O'Donnell did not follow that simple procedure, despite the fact that he did not have any authority to remove those personal effects from Dr. Stakic. My final comment is with respect to what the OTP now claims, which is different from their initial request of the Court. If the Court - and I apologise for summarising this - if the Court would recall that the OTP requested that all letters that Dr. Stakic sent or all correspondence from the Detention Unit to outsiders other than those that were privileged be confiscated and given copies of, if he sent them out, letters, so their handwriting expert can take a sample and make a distinction because it was important to get original documents or original signatures. The OTP insisted that originals were necessary, and by their broad request in their subpoena, admirably convinced this Chamber to issue that subpoena. They have those records. Now, curiously enough, they claim photocopies are sufficient and adequate to meet with their expert. We from the Defence can only say we look forward to reading the experts' opinions and also to be given an opportunity to cross-examine this expert on his protocol, in connection with some of the statements offered by the OTP to this Chamber previously and here today. In summation, if I may, Your Honour, we would respectfully suggest that the OTP has not rebutted any of the foundation issues that we raised in connection with these documents. They have not, as suggested last week, provided the Court with any analysis which would state that the policy of the ICTY investigators is not only to incarcerate and to arrest an individual but also to strip him of his personal effects, that policy has not been brought forth. They have not provided us with a logical explanation which would lead one to even infer that the documents in their possession were remotely properly, ethically and legally inventoried. And therefore, we believe that the bases we're providing to the Court should be granted and the objection should be sustained and the documents not be admitted into evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe that the opinions have been exchanged exhaustively. The Trial Chamber will decide as soon as possible on this issue. I have to admit one omission. The registry just informed me that documents with the provisional numbers S190 to S208 were not finally admitted. We took into account the objections by Mr. Lukic given the 9th of July, but following our policy on the admission of evidence, these documents are hereby admitted into evidence. Furthermore, we had to decide on the Prosecution's fourth and fifth notice for admission of transcript pursuant to Rule -- and video, to Rule 92 bis. We take into account that the Defence opposed and objected the 22nd of July, I think it was page 59. But for the reasons given earlier and in the beginning of this case, we can't see a fundamental reason not to admit this evidence, and we can't see any kind of added value to hear the witnesses listed there as live witnesses. So it -- these documents are admitted, the statements and the video, are admitted under Rule 92 bis. And I think it was agreed that Witness 40 will be heard as a live witness here in court. Any other urgent matters to be resolved before we have court recess? So please alert us in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just was going to inform the Court that this witness, I think you saw in the proofing note, did bring a video with him. A translation has been done of just the portion of the videotape where Dr. Stakic is speaking. It's about a minute long. But no transcript has been done of the entire tape, I'm not sure we're even going to do that of the entire tape which is probably more than an hour or an hour and a half. But I would like to play, while the witness is here, sometime, probably tomorrow, that videotape, the one minute where Dr. Stakic is speaking. And I have provided the Defence, and I believe the registry, a copy of the one-minute extract from that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. From the Defence, any observations in preparation of the following days of this week and the beginning immediately after the court recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. We actually continue -- we do not object to the OTP providing the limited version of the tape, although we haven't been given the opportunity to review it, we did get what I think is a summary or at least an attempt of a verbatim translation of the tape so we did review that today. So they may, with your permission, obviously proceed in that manner. We do, however, have two additional points to make, which we think are somewhat critical for purposes of both the Defence preparation and in light of the fact that we would have approximately three weeks "summer break." And that involves our discussions that we've had at numerous occasions both in court and during Status Conferences before the President of this Chamber, namely we continue to insist, and I advised my learned friend of this this morning, we insist that the OTP provide us a complete inventory either through Mr. Inayat, who said he can do it within 24 to 48 hours, and produce to us all of the Crisis Staff decisions or orders that are in their possession, in connection with the time period namely the 30th of April, 1992, through the 30th of September, 1992. We have, although orally been given some indication, the extent of the material we have, we would like a formal response by the OTP if it's their position that we are in possession of all the Crisis Staff documents, that they make that position clear and unequivocal. And if not, we would request this Chamber by way of an oral motion to compel, if you will, ask that they be produced to us no later than the 26th of August this year which would then enable us sufficient opportunity to prepare a Defence, if necessary, in this manner. Likewise, directly related to that are the documents that, as we recall during Mr. Inayat's testimony, that were taken by way of a legal search and seizure of Kozarski Vjesnik, which is the newspaper gazette, that we've seen some evidence of. The Defence is actually hampered by the fact that not only do we not have all the newspaper or articles in connection with Kozarski Vjesnik that were in existence for that time period, no copies of the full and complete set of documents were provided to us. We believe that those documents would be enormously of great assistance to the Defence and to some of our witnesses, both for purposes of proceeding as well as some of our experts in this case. So we would ask, as we have in the past, that both those items in complete be presented to the Defence as required and prescribed by the rules in this Tribunal. If I may just have one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In addition, Your Honour, as our request previously has identified, we would like also the news articles from the newspaper outlet, which was in existence at that time, called Pre Porod, which is the Muslim, if I may be to say, equivalent to the newspaper or some of the newspaper articles that we have seen that were being shared before this Tribunal and introduced in as evidence. Again, our request is only limited to the time period prescribed in the fourth revised amended indictment, and we are only looking for those articles in their possession, which is my understanding that they do have, with respect, that would deal with specifically Prijedor Municipality and the time period prescribed. Finally, although counsel, Mr. Koumjian, and I discussed this briefly, there was a statement made by Dr. Tabeau last week in connection with documents that she relied on. Although the Defence, at this time or at that time, did not anticipate calling a demographer as a potential expert witness in this case, we've rethought that position. We think it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. may be necessary and enlightening. So we would ask that the OTP produce to us some, of course, if not overwhelming to them, the documents that Dr. Tabeau relied upon, specifically, we request that we be given copies of the voter registrar or voter registration forms that she analysed in her report while making this link, and if the Court remembers, it dealt specifically with the methodology that she used in her report last week. We think that would be necessary for our consultant and ultimate expert to review. Likewise, we believe that from Dr. Tabeau's testimony, that they are in possession, namely, the OTP and Dr. Tabeau, of records from the UNHCR and the ICRC, which identifies certain individuals. We think, based on her opinion and expertise or area of expertise, those documents should likewise be provided to our consultant, so that we may make the appropriate analysis for purposes of both completion and verification similar to one of the models that Dr. Tabeau utilised in an annex to her report. Although we haven't discussed it in detail, so we would be making that request, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I realise overall four specific requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I'm not clear if the Defence is now making these requests under Rule 66, which would trigger reciprocal discovery, because they had previously indicated that they did not want to do that. But taking them, may I ask Your Honour to remind me of the four, but taking them from the back the ICRC list I believe is a public list. If counsel can't get that, the list of missing persons, we can provide that, I believe. Regarding the voter registration, I don't think we can provide that. That is a privileged document like most countries' voter registration list that was provided under Rule 70. In regards to the Kozarski Vjesnik and the Muslim publication, well, I'll check on that. I haven't heard of that Muslim publication being in our possession, but I can check on that. The Kozarski Vjesnik, I think we could probably work out some procedure to have a Defence representative go through those in our offices, because we actually have the physical newspapers, not every article has any translation or summary. But we could probably provide a desk for someone to temporarily go through the Kozarski Vjesniks for the indictment period. And as far as the Crisis Staff decisions, I did ask and one of our people on this case has been tasked with preparing a list of all the Crisis Staff decisions. I think I can give that list to counsel by the end of the week. I have to caution, I'm not sure, it'd be very difficult for me to represent with 100 per cent certainty that that is every Prijedor Crisis Staff decision. We will fry to find all of those. One of the problems is that seizures continue to take place, and not everything is translated. But we will make every effort to provide those. I add that caution because I recently was sent by another attorney working on a different case some Crisis Staff decisions that appear to be the same as those we have, but were taken from a different search than any of ours. So it's possible that there are other copies of decisions that we have, and we may have to look at those to see if there's any signatures on those copies. But that I'll try to have by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the decisions by the Crisis Staff in the time limit found in the fourth amended indictment, I think all the participants, including the Judges, are more than only interested in having access to all the material. We heard that you would provide this, and indeed, it would be -- having heard the statement of Mr. Inayat on this issue, it would be appropriate to have an updated list immediately before the end of the Court recess, the summer court recess, and not only an updated list, also those decisions we have not yet in possession for the period limited by the amendment we have before us. As regards Kozarski Vjesnik, I think it's a fair approach to give the Defence the opportunity to have a look through all these documents, these articles in Kozarski Vjesnik. Once again, limited to the time indicated in the indictment, because I want to recall that already in the past, we decided not to admit into evidence all the articles on a certain page of this newspaper, but limited to the possible relevant documents. So therefore, I think this has been resolved by the invitation of the OTP to look through the documents of the Kozarski Vjesnik from that period of time. I'm more reluctant as regards the -- sorry to call it, Muslim newspaper, because I couldn't find the name on the transcript. Here, we have to take care not to go into a fishing expedition. And once again, I have to recall that tu quoque is not a defence in this case. As regards Dr. Tabeau, finally, I think it would be fair and realistic for the OTP to provide a list of documents they asked Dr. Tabeau to provide when coming a second time as a witness and to provide us with the document in due time before her second statement. The UNHCR and ICRC documents, indeed, they are public domain, and they are accessible. But we heard from Mr. Koumjian that, in case there would be a problem for the Defence, the OTP is prepared is provide these documents. But I think there shouldn't be a real problem as regards these documents. The most crucial point of all the documents mentioned are indeed the Crisis Staff decisions in the period of time. Any further observations in preparation of this week, and let us know what is your intention as regards the witnesses of this week? I know we have the videoconference on Thursday. The witness before us takes three days?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would think that this witness will probably take three days. I'll finish the direct examination some time tomorrow, and I imagine there will be a lengthy cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just want to correct one thing, when counsel mentioned UNHCR and ICRC, I think the list is ICRC, the list of missing persons. We would not be able to get UNHCR documents. We don't have access to those, and they are quite strict on their -- providing their documents to criminal Tribunals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Some are, indeed, published. No doubt that they have, put it this way, a very strict policy not to disclose some material for the one or other reason we have not to judge upon. But of course, in general, just saying UNHCR material is not enough. I think if there are certain documents of probative value for this case, the Defence need to identify these documents, document by document, and not only relating to those documents in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, my request for the UNHCR documents were based solely and specifically on the testimony of Dr. Tabeau, although I don't have her transcript before me. On one occasion, specifically, she identified, during her direct examination, that she relied and reviewed documents from the UNHCR. And it is those documents that we would expect and contemplate our potential demographer would likewise need in order to perform his analysis and evaluation on those issues. Likewise, although I understand the Court's ruling, just so that the issue does not raise its head, are the voter registration or the voters registries, a copy of which will not be provided to us pursuant to our request or, as in our request, we did need that because it is a critical secondary source, in our opinion, that should be used in the methodology for evaluating these statistical demographic figures that were brought to the Court. And since those were the only two, and I understand they don't have the census, just the results of the census, we think that the voter registration would be just as important having -- being identified as the only source available for our consultant and expert to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And to the extent that it is confidential -- I apologise, Your Honour. To the extent it is confidential, the Defence as they have from time to time when instructed and ordered by the Court and when requested by the OTP, we certainly would not disseminate any of this information outside of the auspices of the Defence team and our consultant who would be reviewing it and providing his or her analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. When speaking about public domain, I referred to those documents in part they are indeed even published on the internet. No doubt, that the vast majority of these documents are confidential, and measures have to be taken that they be kept confidential. Nevertheless, I think it's appropriate to forward this request to Dr. Tabeau, and it will then be for the OTP to answer whether or not this material is in the possession of the OTP because if -- I think it's fair that the basis for that what is presented to us can be contested or we are aware of this basis, I'm only afraid that we'll hear once again the answer that for this portion and for that portion, one of the other two members of this expertise or preparing this expertise are responsible. But nevertheless, this shouldn't be a real problem because the underlying figures, they should be made available for the parties and the Judges, as you can probably also identify on the basis of the line of questions by the Judges to Madam Tabeau. But I think we know now where we are, and it's enough for the purpose of preparation of the week immediately after the court recess. And there shouldn't be any delay due to the fact that, in the meantime, no attempt was made to find and analyse the document requested on a fair basis by the Defence. Is it correct that we can continue now with the testimony of the witness before us? Then may I ask the usher to escort the witness in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the Registrar, I will be requesting S213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I apologise for the delay. And the OTP may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Sivac, about the events of the 30th of May, and you talked about the police entering your apartment. Were there other occasions, before you were taken to Omarska, where the police came to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, quite frequently, not only the police but military groups.
