Various people, soldiers, would enter flats, not only mine but also Mr. Safet Ramadanovic's flat just below mine, because we were the two only Muslim families in that building. And they were allegedly searching for weapons which, of course, we didn't have. But I think this was just their farcical excuse to enter our flats, check for valuables, and take them off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did they search the apartments of Serb families in your building the same as they searched the apartments of Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, of course not. Serb families were protected, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness S213.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Talking about the events of the 30th of May, you talked about the mosques that were attacked. I'd ask that you look at this document, S213, and tell me if you recognise, in the photographs surrounding the map, any of the buildings or any of the areas, because some are just areas with no building.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, roughly, photo number 6, this photo here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I think this is the old town with a couple of new houses. This photo was taken recently, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So, where was the mosque in Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The mosque in Stari Grad was in the centre. I think on this very plot of land, one of these here in the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating photograph number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the other photographs? Do you recognise anything depicted?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Photo number 7, I think this is the mosque in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness is actually pointing to number --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: -- The remains of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness is pointing to number 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How about any others?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It's a bit more difficult because I had not been to Prijedor since 1992. And many things happened and changed in terms of urban planning there, in the different sections of the town. I think this is the Stari Grad area as far as I can recognise overgrown with grass. Photo number 11, this one here, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. How about number 10? You had your pointer on that before. Do you recognise that area at all?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This photo was taken from a very peculiar angle, so believe me when I say that I'm not able to identify this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, I really can't. I'm sorry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. How about photograph number 4? Again, it's -- not much is depicted, but do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I think -- I think -- photo number 4. This is the area where the town mosque used to be in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that the mosque that you spoke about earlier in your testimony that you saw destroyed, the town mosque?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was burnt down on the 30th of May, 1992, around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did that mosque have another name that you can think of?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We used to call it the town or the Carsija mosque. It was in the centre of Prijedor town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going to skip in time a little bit, but while we're discussing this subject, in late August 1992, were you back in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, did you see the Catholic -- was there a Catholic church in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a Catholic church in Prijedor. It was -- it was renewed, renovated about ten years prior to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to it in 1992, after your return to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It was during one night when two explosions woke up the citizens of Prijedor. On many houses, glass was shattered and windows, too, and we didn't know what was going on. It was only in the morning, the morning after, that we heard from casual passers-by that the night before, the Catholic church had been destroyed, as well as one of the most beautiful mosques in this part of Europe which was in the Puharska neighbourhood. Let me just add that the mosque was quite new. It had been built just barely years prior to 1992, and it really was a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see the Catholic church or the Puharska mosque after that night that you heard the explosions?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, several days later. I must clarify this to Your Honours. After the release from the camp, persons who had been released from the camp were maltreated and persecuted like dogs. There were several murders, too, where people who had left the camps in Omarska and Keraterm were killed. One such killing took place in a street, Ivica Peretin, a Croat, a friend of mine was killed who had spent the whole period in Omarska. On my way to Puharska where, from time to time, I stayed with my family at some friends' place, my wife's friend, who was a Serb, and she was some sort of a guarantee for us that we will be protected. I saw her outside the Catholic church in Prijedor, Dule, Dusan Miljus, who was an engineer, a civil engineer in the Ljubija iron ore mine, I saw Veljko Hrgar, who was an architect and the head of an architecture design bureau in Prijedor, and several other people, operating a crane, a huge crane used for construction trying to -- the belfry of the Catholic church, it was nearly destroyed, but there were some stones still left intact, and they were trying to raze it to the ground and destroy it completely. When I went to see my friends in Puharska, I saw that glass and windows in their houses -- on their house was shattered, and they took me to see the remains of the mosque in Puharska. It had been razed to the ground, and unfortunately, in that explosion, my dear friend Zijad Kusuran and his wife, who lived just very close to the mosque, were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go to the events of the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour is going to take a break at -- what time would be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Going to the events of the 10th of June of 1992, what happened to you that day?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, on that day, Bato Kovacevic, an active-duty police officer, and another lad we called Brkin in the town who was a reserve police officer came to my flat. But before I get to that, let me just mention that on the same day in the morning hours, my neighbour Safet Ramadanovic and I were having coffee together. He lived in the same building. Rade Strika and a couple of other policemen I did not know came over and arrested Safet Ramadanovic and took him to the SUP building. In a short while, I looked from my window and saw that at a side entrance to my building, the police were taking Omer Kerenovic away. He used to work at the municipal court in Prijedor for a long time as a criminal law judge, and then after another hour, they came for me, too. They took me to the SUP building and ordered me to go to the yard outside the Prijedor SUP building. I was surprised when, in the police van, I found Safet Ramadanovic, my neighbour. Omer Kerenovic, the judge, and Ivica Muntijan, a Croat, who worked at the municipal court in Prijedor. He was a maintenance worker. Soon after, Tomislav Stojakovic and Rade Bolta, the people who escorted us, joined us in the van and took us in the police van to Keraterm. At the gate there, Zoran Zigic, a lad whose last name was Lajic, he was a well-known criminal in Prijedor, waited for us there. And then on the way in, they tried to get Omer Kerenovic into the van because he had tried them a long time ago for their criminal acts and they wanted to cut his throat. Our escorts, Tomislav Stojakovic and Brane Bolta were very correct on that occasion, and they managed to get the van as far as the administration building in Keraterm, and they managed to take us up the stairs to the first floor where we remained and waited until all the paperwork was done concerning our admission to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you go actually to the Keraterm facility or to the military facility that was across the road?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, we went to the administration building in Keraterm. We sat there for about half an hour, perhaps an hour. Time went by very slowly. And then at the door of one of the offices, Gostimir Modic, a man I used to know quite well, he had worked with me in the security services, he was an inspector, and Zivko Jovic, also an inspector for the Prijedor SUP turned up. They told our escorts that we were not needed in the Keraterm camp, but rather that they had agreed with their chief, their boss, Ranko Mijic, for us to be transferred to the Omarska camp. Not much later, we were taken back to the police van. However, in the meantime, our escorts had transferred the Kombi very close to one of the boxes in Keraterm from which they started taking out people and the guards who happened to be there threw these people in the back, into the back of the van. Those people moaned and groaned which probably meant they were being severely beaten as they were being taken out and thrown into the van. When the guards finished with their action, they told our escorts to take us in the van to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you then travel from Omarska -- excuse me, from Keraterm to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was to find out later that we were actually some of the first prisoners to be taken by the main road from Prijedor leading to Banja Luka to be taken to Omarska, down that road. And later, as I talked to my fellow inmates, most of them had been brought to Omarska by country roads. And they clearly understood why. Because the road from Prijedor to Omarska, when you head down from Orlovci, which is there, we saw a horrible sight. On either side of the main road, we used to refer to as the highway, pieces of furniture were lying scattered, cattle killed, various objects. So, our escorts driving the police van, they had to drive a slalom in a manner of speaking, they had to slalom among these objects. When you reach a suburb of Kozarac, when we reached that point, almost all the houses were destroyed and on either side were pillars of smoke rising. So the areas where the houses were burning, soldiers were coming out driving tractors and horse-drawn carts, taking away household appliances and different electronic devices. The crossroads dividing Kozarac from Trnopolje, we saw two tanks with soldiers covered with blood. They were Serb soldiers probably heading towards Kozarac or towards Trnopolje. Those horrible images stretched all the way to Jakupovici, almost all the way to the border line between Omarska, Kozarac, Kozarusa, and Kamicani, all the other villages there, inhabited mostly by Muslims. Kozarac and the surrounding area had the appearance as if an atom bomb had been dropped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be given S14. If that could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, again, the print is very, very small on this map. But can you locate the approximate location of the Keraterm camp on the map?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The Keraterm camp is here, in this area, near the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road. Cirkin Polje is here, and the camp was there more or less, as far as I can tell. It's very small indeed, but it's in this area here, on the left side of the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating the eastern part of the city along the road marked in red that runs east/west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you trace for us the approximate route that you took to the Omarska camp. And tell us where it was that you saw the events that you talked about in your testimony, just previously.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We travelled along this portion of the road, and as early as here, near Gornji Orlovci, on this side of the road, we saw houses on fire. In this area here, this here as well. When we passed Kozarac and Kamicani, we saw again houses on fire. And this is how we reached the junction leading off to Omarska, and we went along this road here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And then which road did you take from that junction? You took the road marked in yellow down, or orange? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, this -- along this orange-coloured road near the overfly. And this is where the entered the Omarska mine complex, through the main gate to the camp. Immediately after you pass the railway line, and this crossroads here, that is where the main gate to the Omarska mine is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you: If a person was living in Omarska or travelling regularly between Omarska and Prijedor, would the route you took be the most typical route for a person to travel? In other words, along that road that runs alongside Kozarusa, Kozarac, Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the best route you can take. And the road was very good. It was recently built, and everybody took that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be possible to travel on that road without seeing the destruction of the houses that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, of course not. It was so obvious that it was impossible not to see it if you went along this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened when you got to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: In the Omarska camp, we were welcomed by the people there. First, they took out the people from Kozarac, from one of the vans, and lined them up against the wall next to the administration building. They immediately started beating them. And after this procedure, after this severe beating of the people from Kozarac, they took them in the direction of the so-called white house. Actually, at the time I didn't know what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these various facilities were called. But when the turn came to my group where Safet Ramadanovic was and others, they ordered us as well to line against the wall. In the meantime, Tomislav Stojakovic who escorted us to the camp gave a list of names to Miroslav Kvocka who happened to be there when the detainees were arriving. So he took this list and went away. I didn't know where he went. But after his departure, people started -- they started beating people again. Safet took out some money from his pocket, but they didn't seem to be satisfied. And they said: "Safet, you've brought only very little money to the camp. You will have to give us some more." Safet was a very famous private entrepreneur there. He had a catering establishment. Shortly after that, Miroslav Kvocka came, appeared again, and he said: "Who has brought Nusret Sivac here?" And they said: "His name is on the list." And he said: "No, you've made a mistake. You've brought the wrong person to the camp. It's her sister's name that's on the list." My sister's name is Nusreta Sivac, the difference being only one letter. And they said: "What do you want us to do with him?" And he said: "Wait a second. Let me check." So, he went away to the administration building and when he came back a few minutes later, he said: "The boss, Ranko Mijic, said you should take him back home," which is what happened. They took me to the SUP building in Prijedor, and I got out there. And they told me to go home. But that night, my sister, Nusreta Sivac, was arrested and taken to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned 5.55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sivac, you just told us about the 10th of June and arriving at the Omarska camp. Do you recall when you first got out of your vehicle what you saw, what your impression was when you looked out at the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: My first impression was terrible. I saw a huge number of people lying down, facedown on the pista. I couldn't tell whether they were dead or alive because nobody seemed to move. I thought they had all been killed. It was only some time later, I mean, shortly after, that I saw some of them move, and I realised that they were alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was the weather like at that time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It was very hot. Really very hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Kvocka told you that -- told the other police that they had made a mistake, and that it was Nusreta and not you that was wanted, your sister. What was your sister's occupation?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: She had been working as a judge at the local court, at the municipal court in Prijedor for a very long time. But after the takeover by the SDS, she was dismissed. She was actually one of the first persons to be dismissed after the takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The people that were at the camp, Mr. Kvocka and the others you saw there, did you recognise them as people you had known or worked with before?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I had known Miroslav Kvocka for a very long time. We used to work together. But I also knew his wife, Jasminka, very well. She used to be my next-door neighbour. She is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were the personnel that you saw in the Omarska camp, were many of them police officers or former police officers from the Prijedor SUP?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: The guards whom I saw for the first time were the people I didn't know. And as far as I can tell, they were not members of the police force at all. They may have been reserve police officers or just people who had been randomly picked up from the neighbouring villages to serve as guards there. Later, I will learn the name of one of them, Miroslav Kos, Kule, and I also learned that he was one of the shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I know that some of this information you learned later, but can you tell us - I know I'm taking this out of sequence - regarding the leadership of the camp, did you know Zeljko Mejakic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a professional police officer who had been working at the Omarska police station department together with Miroslav Kvocka for a while. Drago Prcac would join them later. He used to work at the Prijedor SUP as a crime technician. And I think that he retired some time before 1992. I also knew Krkan, Mlado Radic, who was also a professional police officer. But that's it. I didn't know other guards. I saw them for the first time in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you learn during your stay at the camp who the camp commander was?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. All of the detainees knew that. All the orders and everything that happened in the Omarska camp was in the competence of Mejakic and later, Miroslav Kvocka. The shift leaders who were in Omarska addressed Zeljko as "commander" or "boss," as far as we could tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that after Kvocka said that they had the wrong Sivac, you were taken to the SUP, and then allowed to go to your home. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They allowed me to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sometime after that, did you speak to Milos Jankovic about your arrest on the 10th of June?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I did. I saw him sometime after that, and I asked him who had signed my arrest warrant? And he said that anybody could sign such an order at the SUP, that there was a total chaos there, that most frequently such orders were written by the Crisis Staff and people such as Simo Drljaca, Dule Jankovic, the commander of the police, and even Ranko Mijic who was the chief interrogator at the camp. As for my order, or the arrest warrant for my sister, I don't know. I was never able to learn who signed those arrest warrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to remind us, Milos Jankovic was your boss when you worked for the security service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He came sometime before 1992, several years before that, and he was appointed chief of the communication and encryption centre of the Prijedor SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did you do between the 10th of June and the 20th of June?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: At the time, Prijedor was in a terrible state. There was no electricity, nor water. Military formations frequently searched apartments and evicted people from their apartments. And as a result of these very frequent searches, me and my family were forced to seek shelter in Puharska, where we stayed with a friend of ours. Usually, it was with this lady friend who was Serb. We stayed at her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you feel safer because you were staying with someone who was of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: To a certain extent, yes, but regardless of where we were, the life in Prijedor had turned into a nightmare for us non-Serbs. We had to listen to various types of propaganda on the Prijedor radio against all non-Serbs, and this propaganda machinery by the SDS functioned perfectly. Even Goebbels could be considered an amateur compared to them and what they broadcast at the time. So, it was on the Radio Prijedor wavelength that we could listen to the appeals addressed to Serbs to kill Muslims and other non-Serbs. It was an appeal to lynch all of those who were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it publicly announced who was the leadership of the municipality at that time? Was that ever discussed on the radio? Or who was giving orders for the events in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: All these things happened as a result of the directives issued by the Crisis Staff. Even the chief of the Prijedor radio, Mile Mutic - who was an officer, I think he had the rank of major - at the time was wearing a military uniform. And according to what I heard, he had a military line, telephone line, in his office at all times, that he attended all meetings of the Crisis Staff, and that he even personally invited the population of Hambarine, Kozarac, and other parts of Prijedor Municipality which were predominantly Muslim to surrender their weapons and told them that the Serb authorities would guarantee their safety, and so on and so forth. In those days, the Prijedor radio station was specialised, so to speak, for disseminating and forging biographies, CVs, of eminent residents of Prijedor. It was as a result of the propaganda of the Radio Prijedor that Edo Crnalic, Dr. Eso Sadikovic, Dr. Osman Mahmuljin were killed, because it was over the Prijedor radio, that is, in one of the programmes by Darko Maricic and another individual that a public trial was organised against these individuals. The biography of Professor Muhamed Cehajic was also falsely represented over the Prijedor radio in this manner. And the people who were subject to these misrepresentations and this type of invidious propaganda were later killed or perished in places such as Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to you on the 20th of June?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, they came for me again. It was the same group of people, Ranko Kovacevic, called Bato, whom I had known for a number of years. He said: "Well, it seems that you have to come with us once again. But this time, there is no mistake." So when I got to the SUP building, when I entered the hall there, I realised that Ago Sadikovic, who used to work at the Prijedor SUP as an inspector for white collar crime, had already been detained. Sifeta Susic was there as well, who worked in the criminal evidence unit in the Prijedor SUP. Tesma Elezovic was there as well, the woman who worked at the mountaineer's lodge at Kozara Mount. Several minutes later, Rade Strika appeared at the entrance. He was escorting a young boy, 13 or 14 years of age, and ordered him to join our group. He went to the SUP building, and five minutes later, he came back leading Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, escorting Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, an eminent Prijedor physician. When we were all gathered in the corridor there, he ordered us to get out to the courtyard. It was around noon, and the atmosphere in the yard of the SUP was savage. Two APCs were parked there, there seemed -- it seems as if a orgy was going on in which armed people were taking part. They were arming their weapons and singing Chetnik songs. And when Rade Strika lined us up against the wall there, we were ordered to remove the laces from our shoes and the belts that we were wearing. Members of the intervention platoon for Prijedor arrived, and we were forced to run a gauntlet formed by them. They beat us most savagely with some metal rods or bars, something that I had never seen before. I mean I had never thought that it was possible for someone to beat another fellow human being with such objects. Dr. Mahmuljin fell down as a result of these beatings. Semir Malovcic, the young boy that I mentioned, who was not 18 yet, was crying. He only had a T-shirt on, and I think he had lost one of his boots, so he was barefoot. After that, they pushed us into a basement room, where the detention premises used to be. I know that because I used to work there. And this is where we detained criminals upon arrest. Dr. Mahmuljin couldn't walk. Me and Ago Sadikovic had to carry him in. It was a matter of covering -- a distance of about four or five metres. And when we laid him down on a wooden bench in this detention area, we heard a scream uttered by Dado Mrdja, Zoran Babic, and others. We heard them scream these members of the intervention platoon who said: "The doctor didn't get enough." And they rushed into this detention area like beasts and they started beating us again. But they beat Dr. Mahmuljin the worst, and at one point, he fainted. They hit Ago Sadikovic with this metal rod on his head, and his temple bone was fractured. And all of a sudden, he was covered in blood. And I never thought it was possible for a human being to beat another human being so savagely. Dr. Mahmuljin couldn't move any more. But throughout that time, Dado Mrdja and Zoran Babic kept shouting: "We'll kill you. We'll kill you so you will never get a chance to kill Serb children again." That threat was addressed to Dr. Mahmuljin. After a while, we came out. But before they left, they threatened that they would be back again, and that they would finish us off. In this detention area, after a while, we helped Dr. Mahmuljin, who was gurgling, and he was shouting "my arm, my arm." I think that his left arm was completely motionless. It had been fractured on several places, and Dr. Sadikovic would confirm that to us later on, when we met in Omarska. Sometime later, we were ordered to board a police van which was parked in the yard. Dr. Osman was not a very heavy man, but he was completely motionless. He couldn't move. And Dr. Ago, I, and this young man had to drag him, his feet were dragging on the asphalt, completely motionless. And this is how we put him into this police van. We got into the police van. We got into the back of the police van. The door was shut, so we couldn't see the road that we took to get to Omarska. I know that Sifeta Susic was thrown, as well as Tesma Elezovic into the front part of the van, and they were taken together with us to Omarska. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this boy who was in the cell with you?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: I think his name was Semir Malovcic or something like that. He was from a part of Prijedor Municipality called Raskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you, did he indicate to you how it was that he came to be in police custody?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, we all felt sorry for that young man who hadn't even gun to shave, I suppose. When we got to Omarska, I asked him: "Why in the world did they bring you over here?" And he said that the night before, during curfew in his village, a group of soldiers arrived, raping all the women there, but only the men were later taken away and to the camps. He wanted to help these women, and he ran to the first checkpoint he could reach, near his house, to report this incident to the military manning the checkpoint. However, they, in turn, called the police, and then Rade Strika arrived, took him away, and brought him to the Prijedor SUP, and from there, he was taken to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Only while we were staying together in the garage. Until I got out, until I went to be interrogated and was transferred to the pista, but he remained in the garage. And I really don't know what later happened to him. According to other people's accounts, he went missing in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the part of Prijedor he was from. Is that part of the town of Prijedor or is that outside? Can you repeat the name and tell us where it is.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: It's a part of Prijedor. It's a bit of a suburb, but the name is Raskovac. Here, I can point it out to you on the map if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. If we can go to the video evidence. I think the witness -- do you want to use the other map, the town map, or is this map preferable?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: This map is all right. I think it's all right. I can use this map to point Raskovac out to you, only if you need something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Whatever's easier for you. If you can use the map in front of you, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: All right. That's the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating on the map an area just to the northwest of the populated area looking like Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, it's still S14. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I am going to in a moment going to ask - I'm sorry for the lack of notice - for S294. Sir -- excuse me, 65 ter number 294, and that is -- I'll come back to this tomorrow if necessary. After the 30th of May, was there a -- did events happen in various neighbourhoods of Prijedor that were populated mainly by non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. At that time, an urbicide, so to speak, began in Prijedor. A group of people I used to know, led by Dule Miljus, civil engineer, Veljko Hrgar, an architect and head of an architectural bureau in Prijedor, simply walked the streets formally, predominant Muslim and Croat streets, and they were marking houses to be demolished. A large part of the town of Prijedor was demolished during this intentional action. In the days to follow, when Slavko Ecimovic's group clashed with the Serb military and the police, according to the plan drawn up by the Crisis Staff, parts of Prijedor were to be wiped off the face of the earth, the Muslims parts. So in my immediate vicinity, my own neighbourhood, a Roma people's settlement was pulled down, completely demolished, because they had also lived in Prijedor for hundreds of years. They had blacksmithries. That's how they earned their livelihood. A large part of Muharem Suljanovic Street was torn down also. That's the street to the right of the Bereg area. A part of Zagrad was pulled down. Most of the Stari Grad was destroyed, so that Prijedor seemed like a ghost town without all those buildings which had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On the 20th of June, you talked about at the SUP meeting members of the intervention squad. You had worked for the police for many years. Did this squad exist in the security services, during the years you worked for the security service?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: No, the group called "intervention platoon" was set up for the dirty work to be carried out in Prijedor Municipality. The members of that group were mostly people with a criminal past. People who were outlaws, they had clashed with the law on numerous occasions. And they did their dirty work, the dirtiest work of all in Prijedor Municipality with admirable diligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see members of that squad in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, they did come a number of times to visit the camp. Always accompanied by a number of other persons who would come, who would then give suggestions as to who should be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that two of the members of the intervention squad were yelling about -- to Dr. Mahmuljin, and that one said: "You'll never kill Serb children again." Do you have any idea what he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, how should I say? Just shortly before that, Radio Prijedor published an announcement claiming that Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, while giving medical treatment to another doctor, his colleague, Lukic, from a nearly fatal heart attack prescribed intentionally the wrong sort of medicine to this patient, thereby trying to kill him. This was just not true. This was propaganda, misinformation, only to denigrate Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, to bring him into disrepute and to mark him off for the kill which, unfortunately, later occurred in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after the beating, these beatings, at the SUP? What happened to you and the others?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: We were taken back to Omarska in a police van. They had us lined up again, against the glass wall, the wall of the restaurant. And again, the shift leader, Kurle Kos recognised me and said: "Here you are again. And this time, it's no mistake." Dr. Osman Mahmuljin could not keep standing up against the wall. So he knelt down. And Kos told the guards who assembled like a pack of wolves to beat us again. When he saw the state we were in, he told them: "Don't beat these, just put them in the garage."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And were you then taken to the area of Omarska known as the garage?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes. That day, we were thrown into the garage between 80 and a hundred inmates were already inside the garage from the Kozarac area. And it was crowded enough as it was, and it was very difficult to squeeze new people into the garage. But there we were, practically standing one on top of the other. And close to the iron door in one of the corners of the garage, Professor Muhamed Cehajic, president of Prijedor Municipality, was lying all alone. He had obviously been beaten severely. You could see that he had been maltreated. He urinated blood. I'll never forget that night. Around 8.00 in the evening, the door slammed open, and a Serb soldier appeared. He was wearing red shades. He began to yell and threaten us. He cocked his weapon. Behind him, there were the other guards standing. He was standing at the door and shouting, asking: "Who killed my brother Dukic?" The older inmates answered in unison: "The Muslim extremists led by Slavko Ecimovic, they killed him." He was not happy with this answer, however, and he wanted the answer repeated several times. And then he ordered us to sing. We started singing at the top of our voices. The older inmates, the new inmates, all the Chetnik songs "From Topola to Topola, all the way to Ravna Gora," all those songs, and then also a song that I heard for the first time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it common during your stay in Omarska for the inmates to be forced to sing songs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, very common. They would even tell us that if we wanted to be given a jerry can of water, we had to sing songs. This was common practice in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the general nature of these songs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, mostly these songs abused other non-Serb people living in those areas. They were songs in praise of Chetniks and Serbs in general. Songs very humiliating for Croats, Muslims, and all the other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You told me one of the lines of one of these songs this morning. Can you repeat, please, for the Judges what you remember about the song that you were taught to sing in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to specify. It's a bit vulgar, I know, but please excuse me. I'm not sure if it can be translated. It was one of the guards' favorite songs that we were made to sing. "Early this morning, a Chetnik man was fucking a Muslim woman. There is no guard without the Kokarda," the Chetnik symbol, "and no soldier, if not a Chetnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you find it humiliating to be forced to sing these songs?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was only one of the pressures we were made to face and put up with. We had no choice really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned Professor Cehajic, the president of the municipality. Did you see any other political leaders that you recognised in the camp as inmates?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, let me just finish what I was saying about Professor Cehajic. Immediately after we had finished singing, he was taken out by one of the guards, outside the garage, and beaten very badly. After a while, the door opened again, and Professor Cehajic said: "They want me to collect a hundred deutschmark for them. If I fail, they will kill me on the spot." The camp inmates who had arrived in the camp earlier from Kozarac, no one had anything on them. Dr. Osman Mahmuljin had hidden a hundred deutschmark note in one of his pockets and gave it to Professor Cehajic. And this bank note saved Cehajic's head that night. When Professor Cehajic was taken out of the garage, the guard who was taking him out asked him in a very ironic tone of voice: "So, President, say, where are you now, and where is my neighbour, Stakic?" His accent was strange. He must have been the neighbour of the accused sitting here. He repeated this sentence several times. Professor Cehajic later came back all black and blue, covered with bruises, and he couldn't quiet down for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Had you known Professor Cehajic from your work in -- as a journalist and from living in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Well, yes, you might say I knew him as a professor at the Prijedor high school. It's a very famous high school. He taught literature there for a long time. He also lived in my neighbourhood for a while. We used to see quite a bit of each other, and we regularly greeted each other in the street. He was a very quiet, peaceful man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know -- did you ever ask Professor Cehajic why, after the takeover by the SDS authorities, he hadn't left Prijedor before he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: He had a very good explanation, I think a good one. Airtight for that. He said: "I'd never had a quibble with anyone. The Serbs took over in Prijedor, and there was nothing I could do about that. I never imagined they would commit crimes on this scale. So, I stayed in Prijedor waiting for decisions on a more global level, at the Bosnia and Herzegovina level, decisions affecting the fate of Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what eventually happened to Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Professor Cehajic, the president of the Prijedor Municipality, was taken on the 27th of July away, together with a group of other Prijedor intellectuals, and was killed outside the Omarska camp, in the area of Omarska village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see any other political leaders in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Silvije Saric, a lawyer, was in the camp. He was the president of the Croatian Democratic Union. Then, there was Idriz Jakupovic, who was a member of the Socialist Democratic Party, who used to be a member of the Communist League. Rizo Beglerbegovic, an economist, a member of the reformist forces led by Ante Markovic, and a number of others, other Prijedor residents who were members of the left-wing parties. But it is interesting to point out that the very small number of Prijedor intellectuals were members of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the camp, did you see anyone who was -- had mental problems who was held as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: While I was at the pista, a friend of mine and a neighbour of mine, Asmir Crnalic was with me for a while. We called him "Vico". For a number of years, he had been a mental patient. He had suffered a number of fits. And I was horrified to see that he was there on the pista. During that period of time, the temperatures were very high, and the heat was unbearable. And we often had to all lie down on the pista during those days. One day, we heard a confusion coming from an area inside the camp. And we saw Asmir Crnalic, Vico, there. We saw him stand up all of a sudden, without an approval of the guards. And he had a glass or a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bottle with him, and he pretended to be drinking water. Apparently, he had asked to be allowed to go and drink some water, but the guard wouldn't let him. So, he was pretending that he was drinking water. And he started even spitting at one point in time. And then all of a sudden, he started to dance, to stepdance, on the pista. And the guards started joking and they shouted out to him: "Yes, come on, give us some more." And then one of the guards coming from the administration building grabbed him and took him to the white house. The guard who took him to the white house put him in the first room to the left, and as he was coming back to the administration building, we heard a very short -- actually, two bursts of gunfire. The first one was short; the second was long. We turned around, because we sort of knew what was coming. And then one of the guards said: "Heads down." And we had to lie down again, face down. But we managed to see a guard who was also dressed in a recognisable way. He wore some kind of raincoat with a hood. And he always stood guard at the post between the white house and the administration building. He shot in the direction of the white house. And after we spent some time lying like this face down on the pista, an order came for us to sit down. One of the detainees on the pista stood up, and we could clearly see the body of Asmir Crnalic, Vico, lying motionless next to the white house. Sometime towards the end of this shift, whose leader was Momo Gruban, Ckalja, he came to us to the pista and asked if anyone knew this person. I said I did, and a number of other people who knew Vico. He wanted us to tell him the name and the surname of this man in order to establish his identity. And he wrote this information on a small piece of paper which he carried to the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there a prisoner in the camp who was blind or almost blind?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was actually very sad to see from the pista, Eso Mehmedagic running after the column of the people who were going to the restaurant. He had worked at the Prijedor court for a while, and he was then transferred to the public attorney's office. At one point in time, he would always run at the back of the column of these people. And he was holding the hand of Becir, an engineer who worked to work at the Omarska iron ore mine before. And this is how he went to the restaurant to get a meal. And he would also run like this, in this fashion, on the way back. And the women who used to work at the canteen there told us that the guards would always push him around. Actually, they would push him to the opposite side of the group. They engaged in all sorts of pranks like this with him and ridiculed the man all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said he worked at the court and public attorney's office. Was he a lawyer, an attorney?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Yes, he worked as a defence lawyer for a while. He had a degree in law, and he spent all his life working at the Prijedor court while his sight was still good. Later on, he was transferred to the Prosecution office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him and Becir, the engineer who used to guide him to the meal, to the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: NUSRET SIVAC
utterances.text: Esad Mehmedagic was the first one to be killed. That night, the lawyers were on target in Omarska. They killed lawyers that night, and it was on that night that Esad Mehmedagic was taken to the white house and killed. Later, when they proceeded to killing of the people who used to work at the mine, Zivko Paunovic was killed. Then, sometime from the 25th of July onwards, apart from the daily murders of the detainees who were taken up for interrogation and spontaneous killings perpetrated by the guards on their own, killings of specific -- of members of specific professions started. The first ones on the execution list were the former Prijedor police officer, Mirzet Lisic, Ago Sadikovic, inspectors of the Prijedor SUP were killed together. Ismet Aras, Fikret Sarajlic, police officers, Meho Mahmutovic, also a police officer. Emir Kodzic [phoen], another police officer, were all killed. Only a few police officers would leave the Omarska camp alive. Four or five of them survived, only four or five. After that came the turn of Prijedor physicians, Prijedor doctors. Namely, Dr. Jusuf Pasic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to get to that tomorrow as a separate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can we break for today, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 2.15.
